images.filename: Abandoned Waste Weir at 39.49 miles on Chesapeake and Ohio Canal.jpg
images.caption: An abandoned waste weir, at 39.49 miles, on the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal. According to Hahn, This is an example of the original style of waste weir, made of masonry blocks which would have had wooden boards above it. (Hahn, Towpath Guide, p. 75). This is just a short ways above Lock 26, at 39.49 miles. These waste weirs were mostly replaced with concrete waste weirs around 1909. National Park Service says: "The stone wings of the original wasteweir and contemporary riprap are visible on the river side of the towpath and sides of the creek. The masonry and wood wasteweir was covered over when it was no longer needed, and riprap was placed along the bank below the towpath. This is a preserved example of an original wasteweir, but the majority of the structure is underwater." [1]
images.alt: An abandoned waste weir, at 39.49 miles, on the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal. According to Hahn, This is an example of the original style of waste weir, made of masonry blocks which would have had wooden boards above it. (Hahn, Towpath Guide, p. 75). images.filename: Bypass Flume Lock 7 C and O Canal.jpg
images.caption: The bypass flume (flowing behind the lockkeeper's house) on Lock 7, on the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal, at 7 miles on the towpath. The bypass flume allows water to bypass the lock and fill the level (pound) below the lock. Without this, the boats below tend to bottom out because of lack of water.
images.alt: The bypass flume (flowing behind the lockkeeper's house) on Lock 7, on the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal, at 7 miles on the towpath. The bypass flume allows water to bypass the lock and fill the level (pound) below the lock. Without this, the boats below tend to bottom out because of lack of water.
categories: Chesapeake & Ohio Canal National Historical Park

images.caption: This is the basin at the end of the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal, looking north toward the end of the canal. Guard lock #8 is at the end of the channel on the left. Interstate Highway 68 / US 40 / US 220 runs on that bridge in the background. The Cumberland Masonic Temple and the Emmanuel Episcopal Church are visible to the left, beyond the highway bridge. The Western Maryland Station is just visiable (brick building, center of picture) beyond the highway bridge. Shops at Canal Place are to the right of the basin. Potomac River is to the left, just beyond the flood wall.
